newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Virtual store opens in Manhattan.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Virtual store opens in Manhattan.

text.p: To many, the idea of online shopping conjures up images of making purchases by computer from the comfort of home while wearing a bathrobe and fuzzy slippers.
Tuck Rickards, the founder and chief executive officer of Virtual Emporium, hopes to change that image by creating a line of retail stores where customers can come to shop via the World Wide Web.
A store that opened recently on Manhattan's Upper West Side is his second step in that process.

While Virtual Emporium's efforts to bring online shopping out of the house and into the mall may seem counter-intuitive, Rickards points out that for the less-technologically savvy, the idea of solo online shopping may seem daunting.

"One hundred percent of people have shopped in a store, but only 2 percent of people have ever shopped online," Rickards said. "Our goal is to make this process so easy that my mom and dad can start buying groceries and Christmas presents over the Web."

Like the original Virtual Emporium store that opened in Santa Monica, Calif., last November, the Manhattan outlet will feature personal computers that will allow customers to shop the Web via high-speed Internet connections.

The store is organised with a perimeter of "storefronts," or areas that have items available from the various Web sites on display. The displayed products allow customers an opportunity to touch the merchandise, something no at-home online shopping experience can provide.

"If you go up to the kids' area it's like a mini kids' store, while the apparel area has clothing," said Rickards. "The goal is to try to recreate a mini version of a speciality store for each category."
The actual shopping area is in the middle of the store, with 12 computers where shoppers can look for online bargains while having a cup of coffee, which the store also sells.
"Coffee, for some reason, seems to be part of the Internet psyche," said Rickards. "It's something people seem to enjoy, so we offer it to them."

The in-store computers are linked to the Virtual Emporium Web site, located at http://www.virtualemporium.com/. The Web site features links to 180 of the most popular places for purchasing goods over the Web.
By Rickards' estimate, the Virtual Emporium site gives online shoppers access to more than five million products, including Web bookseller Amazon.com's more than 2.5 million available titles.
"There's no other store that has five million products," said Rickards. "It would take two city blocks to house all this stuff."

Rickards said that some of the most popular items include apparel available through Spiegel's online catalogue, compact discs from the Music Boulevard site and computer equipment sold by the Internet Shopping Network and Gateway 2000.
To make the online shopping experience easier, the Virtual Emporium stores have staff who can help novice Net shoppers find what they are looking for.
The stores also aim to make online commerce more friendly, by allowing shoppers to bring their friends.
"There's part of our psyche that's geared toward a social shopping experience," Rickards said.
"We're trying to recreate the fun of wandering a marketplace in France or going to the mall on a rainy Saturday afternoon in Minnesota."

There is no charge for using the Virtual Emporium Web site. Rickards says the site is currently making money from companies that pay for special product promotions, as well as from limited sales of merchandise directly from its retail stores.
